record.paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
record.original_question: Theorem 3 states that a ℤ_+-valued random vector X is a joint mix with joint center N if and only if it can be written as X = ∑_{k=1}^N X_k, where each X_k is a binary multinomial random vector. Can this decomposition be used in a nontrivial way to characterize additional classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions, and if so how?

evidence.quote: Theorem 3. Suppose that X takes values in Z+. X is a joint mix with joint center N ∈ Z+ if and only if it has the following representation X = ∑_{k=1}^N X_k, where X_k, k = 1, . . . , N are binary multinomial random vectors.
Open Problem 3. Is Theorem 3 helpful (and how) in characterizing more classes of CM and JM distributions?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. A random vector $\mathbf{X}=(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(d)})$ taking values in $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$ is called a joint mix with joint center $N\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ if its components are (in general) non-degenerate and $X^{(1)}+X^{(2)}+\cdots+X^{(d)}=N$ almost surely. A binary multinomial random vector is a random vector taking values in $\{0,1\}^d$ whose entries sum to $1$ almost surely (equivalently, a one-trial multinomial vector that puts a single $1$ uniformly or non-uniformly among the $d$ coordinates). A tuple of univariate distributions $(F_1,\dots,F_d)$ is called jointly mixable (JM) if there exist random variables $Y_1\sim F_1,\dots,Y_d\sim F_d$ on a common probability space such that $Y_1+\cdots+Y_d$ is almost surely constant; a single distribution $F$ is called $d$-completely mixable ($d$-CM) if $(F,F,\dots,F)$ ($d$ copies) is jointly mixable.

Known representation. A $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$-valued random vector $\mathbf{X}$ is a joint mix with joint center $N$ if and only if it admits the representation
$$\mathbf{X}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbf{X}_k,$$
where $\mathbf{X}_1,\dots,\mathbf{X}_N$ are (not necessarily independent and not necessarily identically distributed) binary multinomial random vectors on $\{0,1\}^d$.

Problem. Determine whether the above binary-multinomial decomposition can be used in a nontrivial way to characterize further classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions beyond those currently known. Specifically, exhibit (or rule out) new families of univariate distributions $F$ (or tuples $(F_1,\dots,F_d)$) for which complete mixability (respectively joint mixability) can be established or excluded by means of constructing or obstructing an appropriate decomposition into binary multinomial summands, and provide an explicit characterization of such new families together with the constructive coupling implied by the decomposition.
artifact.status_search_result: A full characterization of completely mixable and jointly mixable distributions is known only for $n\le 2$; for $n\ge 3$ the problem remains open, and no published work appears to have leveraged the binary-multinomial decomposition theorem to characterize new classes of CM/JM distributions. Subsequent work on detecting and on elliptical/related families of joint mixability does not address this specific question.

status_evidence.title: Current open questions in complete mixability
status_evidence.snippet: Open Problem 3. Is Theorem 3 helpful (and how) in characterizing more classes of CM and JM distributions?
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly listed as an open problem in the survey on complete mixability.

status_evidence.title: Detecting complete and joint mixability
status_evidence.snippet: For n = 1 or n = 2 the sets of jointly mixable and completely mixable distributions are fully characterized; for n >= 3 a full characterization remains an open question.
status_evidence.claim: No general characterization of CM/JM distributions for n>=3 is available, and subsequent literature does not resolve the binary-multinomial decomposition question.
